result:
Lichen is the thing I keep coming back to. It looks like nothing, a gray-green crust on a gravestone, a smear of orange on a boulder, and it turns out to be one of the stranger arrangements in biology. A lichen isn't a single organism. It's a fungus that has taken up farming: it houses algae or cyanobacteria inside its body, gives them shelter and water, and lives on the sugar they make from sunlight. Neither partner looks anything like the lichen when grown alone. The form only exists in the partnership.

What I like most is the pace. Some lichens grow less than a millimeter a year. A patch the size of a dinner plate on an Arctic rock may have started before the Roman Empire. Geologists use this, measuring lichen diameters to date when a glacier retreated or a rockslide settled, which means a crust most people step over is working as a clock.

They are also tough in a way that seems unreasonable. Lichens have survived exposure to open space on the outside of the International Space Station. They colonize bare lava, and by slowly breaking down the rock they begin the process of making soil, which everything after them depends on. Yet they're sensitive to air pollution, so much that their disappearance from city trees was an early warning about sulfur dioxide.

There's something appealing in an organism that is patient, cooperative, tough, and almost entirely ignored. The next time you pass an old stone wall, look closely.
